newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Apr 4.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Apr 4.

text.p: The tables were turned on Parliament's perk-buster, ACT NZ's Rodney Hide, on Thursday as National and Labour MPs ganged up to attack his campaign and accuse him of hypocrisy. The scrap occurred as Hide quizzed Parliamentary Service, the controller of MPs' expenditure, during the government administration select committee meeting. In a rare show of unity, committee members from National and Labour moved to stall Hide's attack. Page 1.

The elderly may have to live well beyond 65 to get national superannuation if New Zealand continues with its present scheme, Prime Minister Jim Bolger said. Bolger told a Government to Business Summit meeting in Wellington on Thursday that New Zealand could not avoid the demographic trend of an aging population but it could increase the retirement age. Page 2.

Some of the excesses of the heal reforms "remind me of Richard Loe on a bad day", Associate Health Minister Neil Kirton says. Kirton said one example was the public-private bid for cardiac services in the South Island, when a "sane, sensible solution would have been for the Otago and Christchurch CHEs to get together and come up with a joint public bid." Page 2.

New Zealand risks losing more business to Australia if it does not refine labour laws, according to Labour Minister Max Bradford. Bradford told the Government to Business Summit that radical labour market reform in Australia posed a real threat to New Zealand's relative competitiveness. "The Australian workplace legislation is almost as good as our ECA Employment Contracts Act, with all the productivity increases and improved competitiveness this implies." Page 2.

The Coalition Government's transition period was over and was bedding in, despite some minor hiccups along the way, PM Bolger said on Thursday. Opening the Government to Business Summit, he said it was a good time to be talking business. "Maybe there have been a few too many hiccups along the way but, overall, nothing like the difficulties that were predicted by many commentators and political opponents," he said in his prepared speech. Page 2.

Conservation Department staff were now contemptuous of top management and wanted restructuring put off because they feared for the department's future, Public Services Association delegates told director-general Bill Mansfield on Thursday. But the department said on Thursday night that changes had to be made quickly to improve its ability to deliver quality conservation work. Page 2.

The size and role of government in the economy is still too big and there needs to be more private enterprise competition for government services, according to Commerce Minister John Luxton. The government would look at the help it gave industry, and the value for money of Tradenz and the business development boards, Luxton said on Thursday. Speaking at a government-to-business summit in Wellington, Luxton said: "At one-third of the economy, the role of government is still too large." Page 13.

Nestle is disappointed its bid for Tip Top Icecream did not find favour with Heinz Wattie, and admits it is the obvious next choice to enter the New Zealand market, but is not revealing any plans. Heinz Wattie sold Tip Top to Western Australian food company Peters and Brownes for an undisclosed sum on Wednesday, as part of a disposal of its non-core assets. Page 13.

Colonial Mutual plans to issue 75 million new share and option packages as part of its float on the New Zealand and Australian Stock Exchanges on May 19. This will add to the 78 million shares already committed for sale. A retail application price of NZ$2.95 is planned in New Zealand, the company said, in issuing the prospectus for the float on Thursday. Page 13.

State asset sales were still possible in the next three years, despite some state Crown assets being "off limits", Prime Minister Jim Bolger said on Thursday. Speaking to a Government to Business Summit in Wellington, Bolger was asked if privatisation was off the agenda for the next three years because of the coalition agreement with NZ First. Page 13.

Australia's Foodland Associated expects 57 percent-owned Progressive Enterprises to improve its second-half contribution, the group said. Foodland reported a 34.7 percent lift in net profit to a record A$28.7 million for the six months to January. "We expect an improved contribution from Progressive in the second half as management further strengthens operating and financial controls, improves margins and further reduces debt through the sale of non-core assets," managing director Barry Alty said. Page 13.

The planned purchase of the Bank of Melbourne by Westpac should not impact on the New Zealand banking environment, WestpacTrust chief executive Harry Price said on Thursday. Bank of Melbourne said it had agreed to a A$1.435 billion takeover bid by Westpac. Page 13.

Food processor Cedenco Foods said that a favourable judgement in its four-year-old dispute with State Insurance may boost the company's pre-tax earnings by $1 million. Cedence claimed $3.26 million, plus interest and legal costs, over State's treatment of the company's crop losses incurred during the 1992-93 season. Page 13.
